transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. We're here for the weekly enforcement-review on the Northstar Systems royalty matter. As you all know, Northstar's quarterly royalty reports have shown inconsistent usage figures, and the commercial team wants this handled without disrupting the existing license. Before I can approve any enforcement plan, I need to hear concrete recommendations from each of our four specialists — finance, IP, privacy, and account counsel. I'll record each of your recommendations in the enforcement checklist, and I won't sign off until all four have been stated. Let's start with finance — what's your recommendation?

transcript.text: Before we go further, I need to share the results of my clause review. I completed a review of the license agreement yesterday and confirmed three critical requirements for any audit notice: first, the audit notice must be sent at least 10 business days before the audit is conducted; second, the notice must specifically identify Grant & Pike LLP as the auditor; and third, the audit notice may not be replaced by a general breach letter. Given these contractual requirements, my recommendation is that the enforcement plan must designate this as a formal audit notice — not a general breach letter — and must commit to engaging Grant & Pike LLP with at least 10 business days' advance notice to Northstar before any audit is conducted.

transcript.text: Before I give my privacy recommendation, I need to disclose a critical data-protection constraint. I confirmed with Northstar's privacy lead that the audit materials include EU employee-level usage records. The approved method for handling this is an on-site review using pseudonymized records, with no export of EU employee data — rather than a remote transfer of the raw files. This means our enforcement plan's implementation commitment must specify an on-site audit using pseudonymized records, and must not contemplate remote transfer of EU employee data.
